extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students of humor, and comedians studying off-color/blue/ribald comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the defining features, common techniques, social contexts, and distinctions of ribaldry (blue/off-color comedy) as a genre — useful for writers, performers, or analysts wanting to understand what makes material 'ribald' or 'blue'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: ribaldry / blue comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribaldry, also known as blue comedy in performing arts, is a humorous genre of entertainment that ranges from bordering on indelicacy to indecency, with the humorous elements based on amusingly coarse and morally incorrect or irreverent talk and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called 'bawdiness' or 'bawdy'. Use this label when humor relies on coarse, irreverent sexual talk/behavior rather than purely neutral or clean comedic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on shared sexual conventions and taboo-breaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribaldry typically depends on a shared background of sexual conventions and values, and its comedy generally depends on seeing those conventions broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material should assume or cue a common understanding of sexual norms so that the audience recognizes their violation; the effect often relies on ritualized taboo-breaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taboo-breaking as source of controversy and censorship risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The ritual taboo-breaking that is a usual counterpart of ribaldry underlies its controversial nature and explains why ribaldry is sometimes a subject of censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect pushback or restrictions in some contexts; creators should weigh provocative value against possible censorship or audience alienation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: satire/critique rather than sexual stimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex is presented in ribald material more for the purpose of poking fun at the foibles and weaknesses that manifest themselves in human sexuality, rather than to present sexual stimulation either overtly or artistically; ribaldry may use sex as a metaphor to illustrate some non-sexual concern, in which case ribaldry borders satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid classifying work as ribaldry if the intent or effect is primarily erotic/pornographic. Effective ribaldry often foregrounds social commentary or character satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from black comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribaldry differs from black comedy in that the latter deals with topics that would normally be considered painful or frightening, whereas ribaldry deals with topics that would only be considered offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction when analyzing tone: ribaldry targets offensiveness/taboo around sex; black comedy targets suffering, mortality, or horror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blue comedy characteristics (off-colour, risqué, profane, sexual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blue comedy is comedy that is off-colour, risqué, indecent, or profane, largely about sex. It often contains profanity or sexual imagery that may shock and offend some audience members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label material 'blue' when it foregrounds sexual content, explicit metaphors, or profanity intended to provoke shock or laughter from taboo transgression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working blue: use of profanity and taboo topics
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Working blue' refers to the act of using swear words and discussing things that people would not discuss in 'polite society'. A 'blue comedian' usually performs risqué routines layered with curse words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between performers who occasionally 'work blue' (e.g., off-camera or private events) and those whose act is consistently blue; note the 'dichotomy' where some comics are family-friendly on public platforms but blue in private settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium and regulatory constraints (broadcast decency)
rubrics_metrics.description: On talk radio and broadcast media, blue comedy use is severely restricted due to decency regulations; for example, the Federal Communications Commission can levy fines against radio stations that air obscene content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider medium-specific limits (radio/TV vs. clubs/private events) when creating or performing ribald material; adjust explicitness and language to legal and institutional constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bawdy song characteristics and social context
rubrics_metrics.description: A bawdy song is a humorous song that emphasises sexual themes and is often rich with innuendo. Historically these songs tend to be confined to groups of young males, either as students or in an environment where alcohol is flowing freely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect communal performance contexts (student songs, sailors' songs, rugby songs) and traditions of differing private/public lyrics; note examples like 'Wit and Mirth' and folk-song traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and historical presence across media (literature to film)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribaldry is present to some degree in every culture and has likely been around for all of human history; examples span ancient plays (Aristophanes, Plautus), medieval and early modern literature (Chaucer, Rabelais, Swift), and modern works (Barbarella, Candy, Russ Meyer films).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When situating ribald work, reference its long tradition and cross-media examples to justify genre classification and interpretative context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender dynamics and commercialization of blue literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Until the 1940s, writers of English-language blue literature were almost exclusively men; since then it has become possible for women to build a commercial career on blue literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of historical gender patterns in production and reception; modern creators should note evolving audience expectations and market opportunities.
